lessonPlan.title: The Tell-Tale Heart unit
lessonPlan.author: Edgar Allan Poe
lessonPlan.editionNote: Reading text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Works_of_the_Late_Edgar_Allan_Poe_(1850)/Volume_1/The_Tell-Tale_Heart (revision 14833580), cleaned for Liber et Libri.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 7–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Tell-Tale Heart.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Tell-Tale Heart: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does The Tell-Tale Heart suggest about guilt and conscience?
What does The Tell-Tale Heart suggest about the unreliable mind?
What does The Tell-Tale Heart suggest about obsession?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

lessonPlan.differentiation: Every prompt and quiz has eleven rigor levels (Middle School through Graduate / PhD); the app applies student override, then class standard, then the automatic level. Each prompt is tagged for Common Core, Indiana 2023, Dual Credit (Indiana College Core), AP and Cambridge where they apply.

syllabus.readingLoad: 1 parts of the story in 1 90-minute lessons (90 minutes)
activities: Daily 90-minute lesson: bell-ringer, vocabulary and word histories, background, I do / We do / You do, discussion, exit ticket, closure
Writing prompt at assigned rigor (one graded per week)
syllabus.assessment: Quiz average plus one graded writing prompt

wholeBookTest.title: The Tell-Tale Heart: whole-book test

items.prompt: What does the narrator say drove him to kill the old man?
options: An insult from the old man

items.prompt: How many nights does the narrator watch the old man before acting?
options: Seven, killing him on the eighth

items.prompt: Where does the narrator hide the body?
options: Under the floorboards of the chamber

items.prompt: Why do the police come to the house?
options: A neighbor heard a shriek in the night
The old man's son reports him missing
They are searching for a thief
He finds the old man's will
A beating sound he believes is the dead man's heart

items.prompt: In the line “First of all I dismembered the corpse.”, what does “dismembered” most nearly mean?
options: hiding one's true feelings or intentions

items.prompt: In the line “There entered three men, who introduced themselves, with perfect suavity, as officers of the police.”, what does “suavity” most nearly mean?
options: hiding one's true feelings or intentions

items.prompt: As used in the story (“First of all I dismembered the corpse.”), what does “dismembered” mean?
options: assumptions an argument is based on

items.prompt: As used in the story (“There entered three men, who introduced themselves, with perfect suavity, as officers of the police.”), what does “suavity” mean?
options: a step in walking or running
capable of being borne or endured
hiding one's true feelings or intentions

items.prompt: As used in the story (“"Villains!" I shrieked, "dissemble no more!”), what does “dissemble” mean?
As used in the story (“You should have seen how wisely I proceeded—with what caution—with what foresight—with what dissimulation I went to work!”), what does “dissimulation” mean?
options: assumptions an argument is based on
a step in walking or running
hiding one's true feelings or intentions

items.prompt: As used in the story (“And now at the dead hour of the night, amid the dreadful silence of that old house, so strange a noise as this excited me to uncontrollable ”), what does “uncontrollable” mean?
options: capable of being borne or endured

answerKey.answer: Seven, killing him on the eighth
Under the floorboards of the chamber
A neighbor heard a shriek in the night
A beating sound he believes is the dead man's heart
hiding one's true feelings or intentions

shortAnswer: Explain how guilt and conscience develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how the unreliable mind develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how obsession develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (guilt and conscience, the unreliable mind, obsession) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Tell-Tale Heart teaches about guilt and conscience. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Edgar Allan Poe develops guilt and conscience in The Tell-Tale Heart. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Edgar Allan Poe develops guilt and conscience across The Tell-Tale Heart. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Tell-Tale Heart (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of guilt and conscience. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of guilt and conscience in The Tell-Tale Heart. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Edgar Allan Poe's choices in The Tell-Tale Heart (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of guilt and conscience, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Tell-Tale Heart's treatment of guilt and conscience in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on guilt and conscience in The Tell-Tale Heart that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on guilt and conscience in The Tell-Tale Heart. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about guilt and conscience in The Tell-Tale Heart, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on guilt and conscience in The Tell-Tale Heart, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
